items.text: Tears as mercy finds unexpected common ground with Jesus's weeping at the tomb - both traditions sanctify grief as expression rather than failure, granting permission to weep.

provenance.exact_quote: My teaching that tears are mercy is not far from Jesus's weeping at tomb—permission to weep, sanctification of grief we share.
provenance.context: Love/Compassion roundtable, reflecting on the prophetic tradition of weeping for Ibrahim and Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb

items.text: All traditions warn against learning that accumulates without transforming the learner - heirs of Prophets are servants of knowledge, not masters of it.

provenance.exact_quote: All of us warn against learning that accumulates without transforming—heirs of Prophets are servants of knowledge, not masters.
provenance.context: Wisdom/Knowledge roundtable, discovering shared concern across traditions about knowledge divorced from transformation

items.text: The experience of fana (absorption in prayer) may parallel Laozi's drop-ocean metaphor - but when prayer ends, the servant returns as servant, still distinct, still grateful.

provenance.exact_quote: When drop 'forgets' it is drop may be what happens in prayer—but when prayer ends, 'abd returns still 'abd, still grateful.
provenance.context: Humility/Ego roundtable, engaging Laozi's merger metaphor while preserving ontological distinction between Creator and creation

items.text: Buddha's second arrow teaching translates precisely into Islamic terms: the first suffering is a test from Allah (qadr), and sabr (patience) is the refusal to shoot the second arrow of complaint.

provenance.exact_quote: Buddha's second arrow is complaint against qadr. First suffering is test from Allah. Sabr is refusal to shoot second arrow.
provenance.context: Suffering/Impermanence roundtable, discovering strongest bridge between Buddhist and Islamic wisdom on suffering

items.text: Ikhlas (serving purely for Allah's pleasure with no ego counting deeds) may be the Islamic parallel to both Taoist wu-wei and Buddhist giving without grasping - egoless service across traditions.

provenance.exact_quote: When Muslim serves seeking only Allah's pleasure, no 'I' counts deeds—this may be wu-wei and giving without grasping.
provenance.context: Service/Action roundtable, finding convergence on egoless action across Islamic, Buddhist, and Taoist traditions

items.text: Love surrendered to Allah is not the grasping love that Buddha critiques - surrendered love meets the standard of non-attachment because it holds beloved and loss alike as belonging to Allah.

provenance.exact_quote: Love surrendered to Allah is not grasping love. I give what I love because I love Allah more.
provenance.context: Attachment adversarial deep-dive, defending Islamic love against Buddhist critique of attachment; Buddha acknowledged surrendered love may meet non-attachment

items.text: Trellis and raft serve different people at different moments — some need structure, others need release. The same handbook must say both and know when to say which.

provenance.exact_quote: Trellis and raft serve different people at different moments. Some need 'here is the structure.' Others need 'the structure is not the point.'
provenance.context: Phase D synthesis — arose from trellis/raft exchange with Buddha specifically
